newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Cautious optimism for Sierra Leone peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Cautious optimism for Sierra Leone peace deal.

text.p: A peace accord in Sierra Leone's five-year civil war looks likely this month despite serious ceasefire violations last week, diplomats said on Thursday.
Government officials said President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah had increased contacts in recent weeks with Revolutionary United Front (RUF) leader Foday Sankoh, who is in Ivory Coast.
Kabbah's special adviser on peace, Sharka Mansaray, told reporters the president had a hot line to Sankoh. Diplomats said Sankoh could visit Sierra Leone before a final deal was signed.
Although peace talks in Abidjan broke off in disagreement in May, Kabbah's envoys have continued to visit Sankoh in the Ivorian commercial capital, the diplomats said.

"We understand that with international assistance Foday Sankoh will soon be flown from Abidjan to Sierra Leone where he will visit his troops in the bush so as to keep them informed of the peace negotiations," a diplomat said.
"A final agreement between the two leaders should then be signed in Abidjan, possibly in the next couple of weeks," added the diplomat, who asked not to be named.
Mansaray does not discount such reports while not directly confirming an accord is imminent.
"Foday Sankoh has been asking for extensive political, social and economic reforms which we have acceded to," he said.

"We even agreed to set up a trust fund for the RUF to help them organise themselves into a political party. We have done all the groundwork to reach an agreement and there is a fair amount of understanding of each other's position, so it could happen anytime," Mansaray told Reuters.
An Ivorian Foreign Ministry source close to the negotiations brokered by his government said Ivory Coast was encouraging Sankoh to sign a peace accord but gave no details or a date.
Not everyone shares the optimism, as reflected in a sceptical editorial by popular Freetown daily "For di People".

"Foday Sankoh has only been biding his time in his posh Abidjan hotel. The recent surge of RUF attacks surely prove that Sankoh has a different conception of peace than the government or that held by many suffering Sierra Leoneans," it said.

The exact nature of Sankoh's cause remains unclear. Highly critical of the government as a continuation of the corrupt and mismanaged governments of the past, Sankoh has preached a Libyan-style popular revolution, highlighting the need for education and health reforms.

More than 15,000 people have died since RUF launched the war with an incursion into eastern Sierra Leone from neighbouring Liberia. Nearly half the population of four million are homeless, the mining industry that supported many shattered.
The main sticking point in the negotiations has been the presence of foreign troops in Sierra Leone, notably mercenaries of South African security firm Executive Outcomes.
The government army, despite backing from Nigerian and Guinean troops, was handed a series of setbacks near the capital just before the South Africans were called in in May 1995.

They helped the army retake the initiative in the war but their presence now poses an additional problem for the government. Officials say the International Monetary Fund has demanded drastic cuts in payment to the South Africans before Sierra Leone can expect to get $200 million in foreign funding for its post-war resettlement and reconstruction programme.
